Coat 747's own wall: a light, high-albedo coating on its north-east face takes 0.64 K off the peak facade surface temperature and 0.45 K off the mean radiant temperature pedestrians feel below it, for $117,000-$528,000 and no city subsidy. Shading that same wall, which is the reflex move, buys almost nothing (-0.06 K), and the standard fabric fix, external insulation, makes the wall hotter, not cooler.

## Where the heat is actually coming from

The north-east face (it fronts East 41st Street, not Second Avenue) genuinely takes almost no direct sun: its own annual sun-hours average is 235 a year against 1,300 on the west face, and I confirmed it floor by floor. From floor 1 up to floor 25, of the 34-storey tower, this face's excess over air temperature splits as roughly 1.0-1.2 K of absorbed shortwave against 1.4-1.8 K of longwave trapped from the surfaces opposite, with almost nothing relieved to the sky overnight (MODELLED, from the facade attribution solved for this building). Only above floor 25, once the wall clears the streetscape, does the sun start to win. So for most of this tower's height, the wall is not hot because the sun hits it. It is hot because it is looking at something hotter than the sky.

That something is a 45-storey, 145 m tower directly across East 41st Street, [BIN 1037546](hc:building/1037546), built 1928 (MEASURED, NYC building footprints and LiDAR), whose own facing wall sits close enough to this canyon cross-section to dominate what floors 1-25 of [747 Second Avenue](hc:building/1037175) see when they look north-east. It re-radiates what it absorbs straight back at 747's wall, all day, all year.

## What I tested, and the finding that matters

I re-solved the canyon physics three ways for July's peak hour (15:00 EDT), the month this building's facade actually peaks in:

| treatment | facade peak, K | pedestrian MRT, K |
|---|---:|---:|
| coat the tower's wall, albedo 0.6 | -0.64 | -0.45 |
| coat 747's own wall, albedo 0.6 | -0.64 | -0.45 |
| shade 747's own wall, 35% of the beam | -0.06 | -0.07 |
| external insulation on 747's own wall | **+0.41** | **+0.17** |

The first two rows are not a typo. This tier's canyon solver represents the two facing walls of a street as one shared radiative system rather than two independently tracked surfaces, so it cannot actually tell "coat the neighbour's wall" apart from "coat your own wall": either lever moves the same modelled number. That collapses the question you asked into a simpler one, because only one of those two walls is something anyone here can actually paint: 747 owns its own facade and does not own the tower's. The model says coating 747's own wall captures the full benefit on offer.

The external-insulation result is the finding worth sitting with. It is the fabric measure this era of building normally gets prescribed, and here it backfires: cutting the wall's thermal admittance (heavier, better-insulated construction) means less of the net radiation hitting the surface gets absorbed into mass and shed slowly, so the *outer surface* swings harder and peaks hotter, even though it may still cut what reaches the indoor side. It is the textbook case of a fix aimed at the wrong term: insulation manages conduction into the building, and this wall's problem is a radiative exchange between two exteriors.

> This is a July, peak-hour re-solve of a one-dimensional canyon abstraction: it does not resolve two independently temperatured facing walls, has no along-street coupling between blocks, and its air-temperature response is a genuine under-estimate at this scale even where the surface number is solid. Treat the kelvin figures above as the model's honest answer to "what does this lever buy here," not as two separate experiments.

The building's own trigger list never offered a wall coating for this face at all: [747 Second Avenue](hc:building/1037175)'s automated prescriptions treat the north-west, south-east and south-west faces (all solar-dominant) with glazing retrofits, and explicitly say they leave the north-east elevation at full load. That is not an oversight; a coating only earns a place on that list where the model's own rule set sees a solar-dominant floor, and this face never crosses that bar low enough to trigger one. The fix here had to come from a direct re-solve, not the automated list.

This is a private capital cost with no offset in view.
